It may be baffling, but it actually did happen that way. In the latter period before the Civil War, many southern state supreme courts rejected gun restrictions. Most rejected restrictions based on state constitutions with different language. Legally speaking, these are not analogous to the Constitution, and not binding on the Supreme Court.

Immediately after the Civil War, southern states began to pass laws prohibiting black people gun rights. Probably just about everyone knew what was happening, and the 14th Amendment was enacted partially to resolve this problem with gun rights; but ultimately, those laws stood and were never challenged under the 2nd Amendment.

The 2nd Amendment was not established so that Southerners could exercise oppression.

No, of course not, but it was implicated or not implicated as a right so that white people could oppress black people. If it had been challenged by the black laws, I don't know what the outcome would have been.

Once Reconstruction ended, the Supreme Court issued a series of decisions defying the 14th Amendment and developed a doctrine called "selective incorporation." This is where the Supreme Court simply picks and chooses which federal rights are protected from state laws and which are not. This crazy doctrine exists to this day!

In the meantime, gun restriction laws were written and routinely upheld under that very same 2nd Amendment.

In 2008, a new DC law banning the ownership of hand guns throughout the city was challenged and the Supreme Court looked at the issue for the first time ever.

The decision came down 5-4 as we know. On one side, Antonin Scalia for the majority said that the newly-described "prefatory clause" merely describes a purpose and has no actual meaning. On the other side, John Paul Stevens said that the phrase has meaning and the clause means that gun rights attach to the "regulated militia." They went on to battle the whole thing phrase-by-phrase.

The majority cited those state cases I described earlier. The minority actually had federal precedents to cite.

Both sides played around with word definitions and particularly the "idiom" term "keep and bear arms." I don't think either side had it right.

As the contorted arguments from both sides in the 5-4 Heller case infer, there is room for a high-level discussion or debate with points for each side in 2nd Amendment arguments.

Personally, on the exact gun restriction in that case, I think it is quite a stretch to say that people can't own hand guns and keep them in their homes in a major city under the 2nd Amendment -- but not impossible.
